pos: n. (one of the gates of the house of the LORD, on the west)
etymology: Hebrew Shallecheth, a casting out or a felling, from shalak, to cast or throw down; named once, at 1 Chronicles 26:16.
biblical_def: Shallecheth is the name of a gate of the house of the LORD, assigned by lot to two houses of the Levitical porters: “To Shuppim and Hosah the lot came forth westward, with the gate Shallecheth, by the causeway of the going up, ward against ward” (1 Chronicles 26:16). The whole arrangement was settled without favour: “And they cast lots, as well the small as the great, according to the house of their fathers, for every gate” (1 Chronicles 26:13). The chapter is exact about the manning of each side: “Eastward were six Levites, northward four a day, southward four a day, and toward Asuppim two and two” (1 Chronicles 26:17), and “At Parbar westward, four at the causeway, and two at Parbar” (1 Chronicles 26:18). The Hebrew name probably marks the gate by which the refuse and ashes of the sacrifices were cast out of the courts. That the Spirit of God preserved the name of the rubbish gate, and the roster of the men who stood at it, says something about how He reckons such service. The gate by which the filth went out had a guard of Levites set by lot, in wards against one another, and their names are written in Scripture.

corruption_summary: Menial work in the house of God is thought beneath notice; the gate where the refuse was cast out had a roster of Levites set by lot.
corruption_paragraphs: Churches rank their labours, and the work no one sees comes last. The Chronicler names the western gate where the offal of the sacrifices went out, records that its guard was chosen by lot as well the small as the great, and gives the number of men on duty. God did not grade His house's work the way we do.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every post in the house of God is appointed, that the lot removed self-promotion from the assigning of it, and that the humblest station is a ministry in the house of the LORD.

pos: n. (proper name; a chamberlain of Judah whose chamber stood by the horses given to the sun)
etymology: Hebrew Nethan-melek, the king has given, from nathan, to give, and melek, king; the margin of the Authorized Version glosses his title as eunuch or officer.
biblical_def: Nathan-melech is named once, in the account of Josiah's reformation, as the owner of a chamber beside one of the strangest idolatries ever set up in Jerusalem: “And he took away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, at the entering in of the house of the LORD, by the chamber of Nathanmelech the chamberlain, which was in the suburbs, and burned the chariots of the sun with fire” (2 Kings 23:11). Horses and chariots dedicated to the sun stood at the very door of the temple of the LORD, and an officer of the court had his lodging beside them. Josiah cleared the house from the inside out: “And the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the door, to bring forth out of the temple of the LORD all the vessels that were made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven” (2 Kings 23:4); “And he put down the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places” (2 Kings 23:5); and he came at last to the roofs: “And the altars that were on the top of the upper chamber of Ahaz, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the LORD, did the king beat down” (2 Kings 23:12).

corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as a thing outside the church; the sun-chariots stood at the entering in of the house of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: It is comforting to think of false worship as something kept at a distance, in the high places and the groves. Josiah found it at the temple door: horses dedicated to the sun, chariots of the sun to be burned, altars on the roof of the upper chamber, and altars in the two courts of the house of the LORD. The cleansing had to begin inside the gates.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reformation begins in the house of God, that it must reach the roofs and the courts and not only the countryside, and that a king who feared God dismantled what his fathers had built.

pos: n. (proper name; a prince of Zedekiah's court sent to Jeremiah, also called Jucal)
etymology: Hebrew Yehukal, the LORD is able or the LORD shall prevail, from yakol, to be able, with the divine name; also written Jucal.
biblical_def: Jehucal is a prince of Judah in the last days of the kingdom, sent by Zedekiah to ask the prophet for prayer: “And Zedekiah the king sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest to the prophet Jeremiah, saying, Pray now unto the LORD our God for us” (Jeremiah 37:3). At that moment Jeremiah still moved freely: “Now Jeremiah came in and went out among the people: for they had not put him into prison” (Jeremiah 37:4). The same man appears a chapter later under the shortened form Jucal, and he is no longer asking for prayer but hunting the prophet: “Then Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken unto all the people” (Jeremiah 38:1) — and in the verses following they got him put into the dungeon of Malchiah, where he sank in the mire. The verdict on that whole court is given early: “But neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land, did hearken unto the words of the LORD, which he spake by the prophet Jeremiah” (Jeremiah 37:2). A man whose name means the LORD is able asked for prayer and then helped to silence the man who prayed.

corruption_summary: Asking for prayer is mistaken for submitting to God's word; Jehucal requested intercession and then moved to silence the prophet.
corruption_paragraphs: It costs nothing to ask a godly man to pray, and a great deal to obey what he says. Zedekiah's court did the first readily and refused the second entirely, and the very envoy who carried the request for prayer is found a chapter later among the princes who demanded Jeremiah's death. The appetite for religious help without religious obedience is old.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a request for prayer is no substitute for hearkening to the word of the LORD, and that the men who will not hear a prophet often end by persecuting him.

pos: n. (proper name or title; one of the princes of Babylon at the fall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Probably Babylonian; taken as a name or as a court title, perhaps chief of the eunuchs, from the elements sar, chief, and a word for officers.
biblical_def: Sarsechim is one of the princes of the king of Babylon who took their seats in the middle gate of Jerusalem on the day the city fell. The siege is dated with the exactness of a chronicle: “In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, came Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and all his army against Jerusalem, and they besieged it” (Jeremiah 39:1), and “And in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, the ninth day of the month, the city was broken up” (Jeremiah 39:2). Then the conquerors sat down in the gate and gave judgment where the elders of Israel had once judged: “And all the princes of the king of Babylon came in, and sat in the middle gate, even Nergalsharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim, Rabsaris, Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, with all the residue of the princes of the king of Babylon” (Jeremiah 39:3). Several of the names in that list are court titles as much as personal names, and Sarsechim is probably one of them. The king did not stay for the audience: “And it came to pass, that when Zedekiah the king of Judah saw them, and all the men of war, then they fled, and went forth out of the city by night” (Jeremiah 39:4).

corruption_summary: National ruin is explained by politics alone; Jeremiah dates the siege to the day and names the foreign officers who sat in Israel's gate.
corruption_paragraphs: The fall of Jerusalem can be told as a story of great powers and poor alliances, and the telling will be accurate as far as it goes. Jeremiah tells it as a judgment announced beforehand and then executed on a dated day, with the names of the men who carried it out written down. The prophet who had been thrown into a dungeon for saying so lived to see the officers sit in the gate.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God governs the armies of the nations, that His word by His prophets is fulfilled in detail, and that a king who flees by night cannot outrun a sentence from heaven.

pos: n. (proper name; the chamberlain of Ahasuerus who kept the concubines)
etymology: Probably Persian, of uncertain meaning; the title in the Authorized Version is the king's chamberlain, elsewhere glossed eunuch.
biblical_def: Shaashgaz is the officer of Ahasuerus into whose keeping the women of the harem passed after their night with the king: “In the evening she went, and on the morrow she returned into the second house of the women, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the king's chamberlain, which kept the concubines: she came in unto the king no more, except the king delighted in her, and that she were called by name” (Esther 2:14). That one verse is the whole machinery of the thing. The maidens had been gathered by decree: “So it came to pass, when the king's commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought also unto the king's house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women” (Esther 2:8); they were prepared for a year: “Now when every maid's turn was come to go in to king Ahasuerus, after that she had been twelve months, according to the manner of the women” (Esther 2:12); and then, unless called by name, they were kept in a second house for the rest of their lives. Esther went into that system and asked for nothing: “she required nothing but what Hegai the king's chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed” (Esther 2:15). God saved a nation out of a harem, and the book of Esther does not pretend the harem was anything but what it was.

corruption_summary: The book of Esther is read as a romance; Shaashgaz kept the women the king had used and did not call for again.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther is often told as a story of a girl who won a beauty contest and married a king. The text is harder than that. Maidens were taken by royal decree, prepared for twelve months, sent in for a night, and handed to a chamberlain who kept them in a second house, never to be called again unless the king happened to delight in them. Esther was a captive girl in a pagan court, not a bride with a choice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God works the deliverance of His people through circumstances He never approved, and that Scripture reports the wickedness of kings plainly while overruling it.

pos: n. (proper name; the fourth of the ten sons of Haman)
etymology: Probably Persian, of uncertain meaning; named once, among the ten sons of Haman, at Esther 9:8.
biblical_def: Poratha is one of the ten sons of Haman, killed in Shushan on the day the Jews were permitted to defend themselves. The Authorized Version prints the ten names in three short verses, one after another, as the register of an executed house: “And Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha” (Esther 9:7); “And Poratha, and Adalia, and Aridatha” (Esther 9:8); “And Parmashta, and Arisai, and Aridai, and Vajezatha” (Esther 9:9). Then the summary: “The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand” (Esther 9:10). Two things in that last verse deserve notice. The first is that Haman is still called the enemy of the Jews after his death, so that the destruction of his house is set down as the end of an enmity, not a feud. The second is that the Jews took no spoil — three times the chapter says so. This was not plunder, and it was not revenge enriching itself. It was the carrying out of a judgment on a man who had bought a decree for a whole nation's death.

corruption_summary: The end of Esther is charged with vengefulness; the text insists three times that the Jews took no spoil.
corruption_paragraphs: The ninth chapter of Esther is the one readers most often wish were not there, and it is read as a people's revenge. The chapter guards itself. The Jews acted under a decree, on a day fixed by their enemies, against men who had armed to destroy them, and they laid no hand on the spoil — a detail repeated so that no one could call it plunder.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God overturns the device of the wicked upon his own head and his own house, and that His people may defend their lives without enriching themselves by it.

pos: n. (proper name; one of two chamberlains who conspired against Ahasuerus)
etymology: Probably Persian, of uncertain meaning; named with Bigthan, or Bigthana, at Esther 2:21 and Esther 6:2.
biblical_def: Teresh is one of the two doorkeepers of the Persian court who plotted the death of the king, and the discovery of their plot is the hinge on which the whole book of Esther turns. “In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king's gate, two of the king's chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those which kept the door, were wroth, and sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus” (Esther 2:21). Mordecai heard of it and reported it through the queen: “And the thing was known to Mordecai, who told it unto Esther the queen; and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai's name” (Esther 2:22). The conspirators were tried and hanged, and the matter was filed: “And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king” (Esther 2:23). Mordecai received nothing at the time. Years later, on the one night the king could not sleep and called for the chronicles, that entry was read aloud: “And it was found written, that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's chamberlains, the keepers of the door, who sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus” (Esther 6:2). An unrewarded loyalty, written in a book and forgotten, saved a nation.

corruption_paragraphs: Mordecai saved the king's life and was given nothing. The service was written in a book and shut, and years passed. On the night Haman had built a gallows, the king could not sleep, called for the chronicles, and that page was read. Faithfulness that no one acknowledges is not faithfulness that no one recorded.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God in small records and sleepless nights, and the duty of plain loyalty to a magistrate even when it goes unrewarded.

pos: n. (proper name; the third son of Hosah, a Levite porter of the temple)
etymology: Hebrew Tebalyahu, the LORD has purified or dipped, from tabal, to dip, with the divine name; named once, at 1 Chronicles 26:11.
biblical_def: Tebaliah is a Levite of the house of Merari, the third son of Hosah, numbered among the porters who kept the gates of the house of the LORD. His father's house is introduced in the verse before: “Also Hosah, of the children of Merari, had sons; Simri the chief, (for though he was not the firstborn, yet his father made him the chief;)” (1 Chronicles 26:10), and then the brothers are counted: “Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, Zechariah the fourth: all the sons and brethren of Hosah were thirteen” (1 Chronicles 26:11). The chapter begins the whole order: “Concerning the divisions of the porters: Of the Korhites was Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph” (1 Chronicles 26:1), and it explains what the work was: “Among these were the divisions of the porters, even among the chief men, having wards one against another, to minister in the house of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 26:12). A porter was a doorkeeper, and the Chronicler calls his duty to minister in the house of the LORD — the same word used of the priests at the altar. Tebaliah's name says the LORD had purified him, and his office was to stand at a gate.

pos: n. (proper name; one who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah)
etymology: Hebrew Pilcha, perhaps a slice or worship, of uncertain derivation; named once, at Nehemiah 10:24.
biblical_def: Pileha is one of the chief of the people who set his seal to Nehemiah's covenant: “Hallohesh, Pileha, Shobek” (Nehemiah 10:24). The document was no private resolution. It was joined by the whole congregation, down to the children old enough to understand: “And the rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the porters, the singers, the Nethinims, and all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, every one having knowledge, and having understanding” (Nehemiah 10:28). They bound themselves under oath to the law of Moses: “They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes” (Nehemiah 10:29). And the first particular they named was the one that had wrecked them before: “And that we would not give our daughters unto the people of the land, nor take their daughters for our sons” (Nehemiah 10:30). A covenant begins with the sin a people knows it is prone to.

corruption_summary: Marriage is treated as a matter of preference only; the first clause of Nehemiah's covenant guarded the households of Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: Of all the duties the returned exiles could have named first, they named marriage — that they would not give their daughters to the people of the land nor take their daughters for their sons. They had learned from Solomon and from their own fathers what a mixed household does to a nation's religion in two generations. The clause is not racial; the people of the land were idolaters, and the covenant guarded the worship of the home.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the name itself. The principle to recover is that reformation reaches the household first, and that a people serious about God's law puts its own marriages under it.

pos: n. (proper name; the fourth son of Meshelemiah, a porter of the house of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew Yathni'el, God gives or God is giving, from nathan, to give, and 'el, God; named once, at 1 Chronicles 26:2.
biblical_def: Jathniel is the fourth son of Meshelemiah, in the house of the Korhite porters. The chapter opens with his family: “Concerning the divisions of the porters: Of the Korhites was Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph” (1 Chronicles 26:1), and then names the sons in order: “And the sons of Meshelemiah were, Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth” (1 Chronicles 26:2); “Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Elioenai the seventh” (1 Chronicles 26:3). The house of Obed-edom follows: “Moreover the sons of Obededom were, Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, and Sacar the fourth, and Nethaneel the fifth” (1 Chronicles 26:4). These were the men who kept the gates of the temple, and they were Korhites — descendants of the Korah who had risen against Moses and Aaron and been swallowed by the earth. God did not blot out that family. He set its sons at the doors of His house, and gave some of them the psalms. Jathniel, whose name means God gives, is a son of that line.

corruption_summary: A family's disgrace is thought to be its sentence; the sons of Korah kept the gates of the house of God and sang in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Korah rebelled and the ground opened under him, and one might expect the name to vanish from Israel. Instead the Korhites appear generations later as porters of the temple and as the named authors of psalms. God judged the man without destroying the house, and the descendants of a rebel stood guard at the doors of the sanctuary.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's mercy reaches into a judged family, that He gives service to the children of men who forfeited it, and that the gift in any such calling is His.
